claim: Rice resistance to evolutionarily diverse viruses requires Argonaute18 (AGO18).
source: Here, we report that rice resistance to evolutionarily diverse viruses requires Argonaute18 (AGO18).
evidence: Supported by genetic studies showing ago18 mutants are more susceptible to viral infection (Figure 2D-F) and AGO18 overexpression increases resistance (Figure 2G-J).

claim: The antiviral function of AGO18 depends on its activity to sequester microRNA168 (miR168) to alleviate repression of rice AGO1.
source: Genetic studies reveal that the antiviral function of AGO18 depends on its activity to sequester microRNA168 (miR168) to alleviate repression of rice AGO1 essential for antiviral RNAi.
evidence: Supported by data showing AGO18 binds miR168 (Figure 4A-B), AGO1 levels decrease in ago18 mutants (Figure 4D-E), and competition experiments (Figure 5).

claim: Expression of miR168-resistant AGO1a in ago18 background rescues or increases rice antiviral activity.
source: Expression of miR168-resistant AGO1a in ago18 background rescues or increases rice antiviral activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing AGO1a-Res transgenic lines in ago18 background are more resistant to RSV infection (Figure 7B-D).

claim: Stable transgenic expression of AGO18 confers broad-spectrum virus resistance in rice.
source: Notably, stable transgenic expression of AGO18 confers broad-spectrum virus resistance in rice.
evidence: Supported by data showing AGO18 overexpression increases resistance to both RSV (Figure 2G-J) and RDV (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C-E).

claim: AGO1 is a major effector of antiviral RNAi in plants.
source: In plants, it is well known that AGO1 is a major effector of antiviral RNAi; AGO1 associates with virus-derived siRNAs (vsiRNAs) and mediates the degradation of viral RNAs.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: The ago1 RNAi line was much more susceptible to RSV infection and showed more severe symptoms.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the ago1 RNAi line, in which the expression of AGO1s is diminished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), was much more susceptible to RSV infection and showed more severe symptoms.
evidence: Supported by visual symptoms in Figure 1A and Northern blot data showing increased viral RNA accumulation in Figure 1B.

claim: RSV vsiRNAs were readily detected in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes.
source: Northern blot analyses showed that RSV vsiRNAs were readily detected in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes (Figure 1C), suggesting that AGO1 is an effector of vsiRNA.
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data in Figure 1C showing vsiRNAs in AGO1a and AGO1b immunoprecipitates.

claim: AGO1 is an effector of vsiRNA.
source: Northern blot analyses showed that RSV vsiRNAs were readily detected in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes (Figure 1C), suggesting that AGO1 is an effector of vsiRNA.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that vsiRNAs associate with AGO1a and AGO1b complexes.

claim: AGO1s have a role in antiviral immunity under natural infection conditions in rice.
source: Taking together, these data indicate a role for AGO1s in antiviral immunity under natural infection conditions in rice.
evidence: Supported by data from ago1 RNAi lines showing increased susceptibility and vsiRNA association with AGO1 complexes.

claim: AGO18 is a member of a new AGO clade that is conserved in monocots.
source: We have previously shown that rice AGO1 as well as AGO18, a member of a new AGO clade that is conserved in monocots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), is highly induced by viral infection (Du et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic tree in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Du et al., 2011.

claim: AGO18 is highly induced by viral infection.
source: We have previously shown that rice AGO1 as well as AGO18, a member of a new AGO clade that is conserved in monocots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), is highly induced by viral infection (Du et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2011 and confirmed by Western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: AGO18 protein was hardly detectable in mock-inoculated rice plants but accumulated to a high level in RSV-infected plants.
source: Consistent with mRNA expression patterns, AGO18 protein was hardly detectable in mock-inoculated rice plants but accumulated to a high level in RSV-infected plants (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A showing AGO18 protein levels.

claim: RSV infection led to high levels of GUS expression in AGO18p:GUS transgenic plants as compared to the background levels in mock-inoculated plants.
source: RSV infection led to high levels of GUS expression in such plants as compared to the background levels in mock-inoculated plants (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by GUS staining images in Figure 2B and qRT-PCR data in Figure 2C.

claim: RSV infection, but not insect vector feeding, induced AGO18 expression at the transcriptional level.
source: These data demonstrate that RSV infection, but not insect vector feeding, induced AGO18 expression at the transcriptional level.
evidence: Inferred from GUS reporter data showing induction only in RSV-infected plants, not in mock-inoculated plants exposed to virus-free insects.

claim: The ago18 mutant did not exhibit notable phenotypic differences from the WT plants in growth and development.
source: The ago18 mutant did not exhibit notable phenotypic differences from the WT plants in growth and development but were much more sensitive to RSV infection than the WT plants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by observational data comparing ago18 mutant and WT plants.

claim: ago18 mutants were much more sensitive to RSV infection than the WT plants.
source: The ago18 mutant did not exhibit notable phenotypic differences from the WT plants in growth and development but were much more sensitive to RSV infection than the WT plants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 2D and viral RNA accumulation data in Figure 2E.

claim: Viral replication and infection rates increased in ago18 mutant plants.
source: Viral replication and infection rates also increased in ago18 mutant plants (Figure 2E,F, and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data in Figure 2E, qRT-PCR data in Figure 2F, and infection rate data in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: AGO18 may be dispensable for normal growth and development of rice, but is required for defense against RSV infection.
source: These results suggest that AGO18 may be dispensable for normal growth and development of rice, but is required for defense against RSV infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ago18 mutants show normal growth but increased viral susceptibility.

claim: AGO1 is present in the ago18 mutants.
source: Importantly, AGO1 is present in the ago18 mutants.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing AGO1 protein in ago18 mutants (Figure 4E).

claim: The antiviral function of AGO1 depends on the presence of AGO18.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that the antiviral function of AGO1 depends on the presence of AGO18.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ago18 mutants are susceptible to viral infection despite having AGO1 present.

claim: The antiviral activity of AGO18 in the three independent transgenic lines was directly correlated with the expression levels of AGO18.
source: The antiviral activity of AGO18 in the three independent transgenic lines was directly correlated with the expression levels of AGO18 (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2G-J showing correlation between AGO18 expression levels and viral resistance.

claim: AGO18 was not only induced by and functioned against RSV, but also was induced by and functioned against RDV, a double-stranded RNA Phytoreovirus.
source: AGO18 was not only induced by and functioned against RSV, but also was induced by and functioned against RDV, a double-stranded RNA Phytoreovirus (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 showing AGO18 induction and function against RDV.

claim: AGO18 is effective in positively regulating defense against a broad spectrum of viruses with diverse genome structures.
source: This indicates that AGO18 is effective in positively regulating defense against a broad spectrum of viruses with diverse genome structures.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO18 functions against both RSV (negative-stranded RNA) and RDV (double-stranded RNA).

claim: AGO1 and AGO18 evidently depend on each other for their antiviral activities.
source: Given that AGO1 is present in the ago18 mutant and AGO18 is present in ago1 RNAi plant and that both ago18 mutant and ago1 RNAi rice plants were very susceptible to viral infection, AGO1 and AGO18 evidently depend on each other for their antiviral activities.
evidence: Inferred from genetic data showing both ago1 and ago18 mutants are susceptible to viral infection.

claim: Northern blots using RSV RNA2 probes showed much weaker signals for vsiRNAs in AGO18 compared to those in AGO1a and AGO1b.
source: Northern blots using RSV RNA2 probes showed much weaker signals for vsiRNAs in AGO18 (Figure 3A), compared to those in AGO1a and AGO1b (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data in Figure 3A and Figure 1C.

claim: vsiRNAs accounted for about 4.48% of the total small RNAs in RSV-infected plants and 17.37%–9.77% of those in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes.
source: We found that vsiRNAs accounted for about 4.48% of the total small RNAs in RSV-infected plants and 17.37%–9.77% of those in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B), indicating that vsiRNAs are highly enriched in the AGO1 complexes.
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data presented in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: vsiRNAs are highly enriched in the AGO1 complexes.
source: We found that vsiRNAs accounted for about 4.48% of the total small RNAs in RSV-infected plants and 17.37%–9.77% of those in the AGO1a and AGO1b complexes (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B), indicating that vsiRNAs are highly enriched in the AGO1 complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of vsiRNA percentages in total extracts versus AGO1 complexes.

claim: vsiRNAs accounted for only about 2.52% of the AGO18-bound small RNAs.
source: In contrast, vsiRNAs accounted for only about 2.52% of the AGO18-bound small RNAs (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data presented in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: AGO18 is not a major effector of vsiRNAs.
source: These data suggest that AGO18 is not a major effector of vsiRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of vsiRNAs in AGO18 complexes compared to AGO1 complexes.

claim: AGO18 very likely uses a different strategy to regulate antiviral defense response in rice.
source: Together with the finding that AGO18 is required for the antiviral activity of AGO1 (see above), this observation suggests that AGO18 very likely uses a different strategy to regulate antiviral defense response in rice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO18 does not bind vsiRNAs efficiently but is still required for antiviral defense.

claim: RSV infection increases the accumulation of miR168 as well as AGO18.
source: RSV infection increases the accumulation of miR168 as well as AGO18 (Du et al., 2011) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 4A), suggesting that the increased miR168 is not efficiently loaded into AGO1 and hence not effective in targeting AGO1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2011 and data in Figure 2A-C and Figure 4A.

claim: The increased miR168 is not efficiently loaded into AGO1 and hence not effective in targeting AGO1.
source: RSV infection increases the accumulation of miR168 as well as AGO18 (Du et al., 2011) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 4A), suggesting that the increased miR168 is not efficiently loaded into AGO1 and hence not effective in targeting AGO1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO1 levels increase despite increased miR168 levels during RSV infection.

claim: AGO18 recruited a large amount of miR168 in RSV-infected rice plants compared with AGO1a or AGO1b.
source: Intriguingly, from the small RNA deep sequencing analyses, we found that AGO18 recruited a large amount of miR168 in RSV-infected rice plants compared with AGO1a or AGO1b (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1C.

claim: miR168 plays a critical role in AGO1 homeostasis in plants.
source: Given that miR168 plays a critical role in AGO1 homeostasis in plants (Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010) and that the antiviral function of AGO1 requires the presence of AGO18, our observations suggest that AGO18 up-regulates AGO1 by competitively binding miR168 to enable antiviral defense.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010.

claim: AGO18 up-regulates AGO1 by competitively binding miR168 to enable antiviral defense.
source: Given that miR168 plays a critical role in AGO1 homeostasis in plants (Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010) and that the antiviral function of AGO1 requires the presence of AGO18, our observations suggest that AGO18 up-regulates AGO1 by competitively binding miR168 to enable antiviral defense.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO18 binds miR168 and AGO1 levels are reduced in ago18 mutants.

claim: RSV infection of WT rice plants increased the association of miR168 with AGO18 but decreased its association with AGO1a and 1b.
source: Immunoprecipitation (IP)-northern blot analyses further confirmed that RSV infection of WT rice plants increased the association of miR168 with AGO18 but decreased its association with AGO1a and 1b, whereas several control miRNAs (including miR166 and miR156) showed no obvious changes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by IP-Northern blot data in Figure 4B.

claim: Several control miRNAs (including miR166 and miR156) showed no obvious changes in association with AGO proteins upon RSV infection.
source: Immunoprecipitation (IP)-northern blot analyses further confirmed that RSV infection of WT rice plants increased the association of miR168 with AGO18 but decreased its association with AGO1a and 1b, whereas several control miRNAs (including miR166 and miR156) showed no obvious changes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by IP-Northern blot data in Figure 4B.

claim: In RSV-infected ago18 mutants, where AGO18 is absent, more miR168 was loaded into AGO1a and 1b.
source: Consistent with these results, in RSV-infected ago18 mutants, where AGO18 is absent, more miR168 was now loaded into AGO1a and 1b (Figure 4C), which was correlated with the reduced expression of AGO1 at mRNA (Figure 4D) and protein (Figure 4E) levels.
evidence: Supported by IP-Northern blot data in Figure 4C.

claim: Increased miR168 loading into AGO1a and 1b in ago18 mutants was correlated with the reduced expression of AGO1 at mRNA and protein levels.
source: Consistent with these results, in RSV-infected ago18 mutants, where AGO18 is absent, more miR168 was now loaded into AGO1a and 1b (Figure 4C), which was correlated with the reduced expression of AGO1 at mRNA (Figure 4D) and protein (Figure 4E) levels.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4D and Western blot data in Figure 4E.

claim: In the AGO18OE#1 transgenic rice line, in which AGO18 was overexpressed, AGO1a and 1b both increased at the mRNA level.
source: Also in the AGO18OE#1 transgenic rice line, in which AGO18 was overexpressed, AGO1a and 1b both increased at the mRNA level (Figure 4F), likely as a result of more miR168 being loaded into AGO18.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: The increase in AGO1a and 1b mRNA levels in AGO18 overexpression lines is likely as a result of more miR168 being loaded into AGO18.
source: Also in the AGO18OE#1 transgenic rice line, in which AGO18 was overexpressed, AGO1a and 1b both increased at the mRNA level (Figure 4F), likely as a result of more miR168 being loaded into AGO18.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO18 overexpression leads to increased AGO1 levels, consistent with the sequestration model.

claim: AGO2 was induced by RSV infection in wild-type rice plants.
source: Consistent with our previous finding (Du et al., 2011), AGO2 was induced by RSV infection in wild-type rice plants (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2011 and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: Knockout or overexpression of AGO18 did not have an obvious effect on AGO2 induction by RSV infection.
source: Intriguingly, knockout or overexpression of AGO18 did not have an obvious effect on such induction, indicating that the induction of AGO2 by RSV infection is independent of AGO18 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F showing similar AGO2 induction in WT and AGO18 mutant/overexpression lines.

claim: The induction of AGO2 by RSV infection is independent of AGO18.
source: Intriguingly, knockout or overexpression of AGO18 did not have an obvious effect on such induction, indicating that the induction of AGO2 by RSV infection is independent of AGO18 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO2 induction occurs regardless of AGO18 status.

claim: AGO18 specifically up-regulates AGO1 in antiviral defense.
source: Thus, AGO18 specifically up-regulates AGO1 in antiviral defense.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO18 affects AGO1 but not AGO2 levels.

claim: When AGO18 was co-expressed with AGO1a or AGO1b, there was a nearly five fold reduction in miR168 loading into AGO1a and AGO1b and concurrent increase in loading into AGO18.
source: Results from IP-northern experiments showed that when AGO18 was co-expressed with AGO1a or AGO1b, there was a nearly five fold reduction in miR168 loading into AGO1a and AGO1b and concurrent increase in loading into AGO18 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by IP-Northern blot data in Figure 5 from transient expression experiments in N. benthamiana.

claim: The control miR444 was specifically loaded into AGO1a and 1b and co-expression of AGO18 did not decrease its loading into AGO1a and 1b.
source: The control miR444 was specifically loaded into AGO1a and 1b and co-expression of AGO18 did not decrease its loading into AGO1a and 1b (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by IP-Northern blot data in Figure 5.

claim: AGO18 can effectively compete with AGO1 for binding miR168.
source: These data demonstrate that AGO18 can effectively compete with AGO1 for binding miR168.
evidence: Supported by transient expression experiments showing reduced miR168 in AGO1 when AGO18 is co-expressed (Figure 5).

claim: AGO18 contains all of the four AGO signature domains and the DDH catalytic triad.
source: Our analysis indicates that AGO18 also contains all of the four AGO signature domains and the DDH catalytic triad (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by domain structure analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both WT AGO18 and D833A could mostly complement the ago18 mutant for resistance to RSV infection, whereas the YF/AA mutant could not.
source: Based on the disease symptoms (Figure 6C) and accumulation of viral genomic RNAs (Figure 6D), both WT AGO18 and D833A could mostly complement the ago18 mutant for resistance to RSV infection, whereas the YF/AA mutant could not.
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 6C and Northern blot data in Figure 6D.

claim: AGO18 exerts its antiviral function mainly through small RNA binding, rather than slicing.
source: These results suggest that AGO18 exerts its antiviral function mainly through small RNA binding, rather than slicing.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the slicing-deficient D833A mutant can complement ago18, but the binding-deficient YF/AA mutant cannot.

claim: AGO1 expression was elevated by viral infection in the transgenic plants that express WT AGO18 or D833A mutant but not in those that express YF/AA.
source: We found that AGO1 expression was elevated by viral infection in the transgenic plants that express WT AGO18 or D833A mutant but not in those that express YF/AA (Figure 6E), further suggesting that the small RNA binding but not slicing activity of AGO18 is required for its role in up-regulating AGO1.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6E.

claim: The small RNA binding but not slicing activity of AGO18 is required for its role in up-regulating AGO1.
source: We found that AGO1 expression was elevated by viral infection in the transgenic plants that express WT AGO18 or D833A mutant but not in those that express YF/AA (Figure 6E), further suggesting that the small RNA binding but not slicing activity of AGO18 is required for its role in up-regulating AGO1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that binding-competent but slicing-deficient AGO18 can still upregulate AGO1.

claim: The steady-state AGO1a/AGO1a-Res mRNA levels of both AGO1a and AGO1a-Res transgenes accumulated to higher levels relative to the AGO1a levels in wild-type (WT) non-transgenic and ago18 plants.
source: The steady-state AGO1a/AGO1a-Res mRNA levels of both AGO1a and AGO1a-Res transgenes accumulated to higher levels relative to the AGO1a levels in wild-type (WT) non-transgenic and ago18 plants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7B.

claim: AGO1a mRNA level was reduced by RSV infection in the AGO1a transgenic line, whereas AGO1a-Res transgenic lines had no significant reduction in AGO1a-Res mRNA levels upon RSV infection.
source: It is noteworthy that AGO1a mRNA level was reduced by RSV infection in the AGO1a transgenic line, whereas AGO1a-Res transgenic lines had no significant reduction in AGO1a-Res mRNA levels upon RSV infection (Figure 7B), indicating that AGO1a is subject to regulation by miR168/AGO18.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7B.

claim: AGO1a is subject to regulation by miR168/AGO18.
source: It is noteworthy that AGO1a mRNA level was reduced by RSV infection in the AGO1a transgenic line, whereas AGO1a-Res transgenic lines had no significant reduction in AGO1a-Res mRNA levels upon RSV infection (Figure 7B), indicating that AGO1a is subject to regulation by miR168/AGO18.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response of AGO1a and AGO1a-Res to RSV infection.

claim: None of the AGO1a-Res transgenic lines showed notable phenotypic differences from WT or ago18 plants in growth and development.
source: Although the transcript levels of the miR168-resistant transgene AGO1a markedly increased, none of these lines showed notable phenotypic differences from WT or ago18 plants in growth and development.
evidence: Supported by observational data from transgenic plant analysis.

claim: AGO1a-Res transgenic lines were much more resistant to RSV infection than ago18 and AGO1a plants.
source: These transgenic lines, however, were much more resistant to RSV infection than ago18 and AGO1a plants (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by symptom data in Figure 7C and qRT-PCR data in Figure 7B.

claim: Viral replication significantly decreased in the AGO1a-Res plants.
source: Viral replication significantly decreased in the AGO1a-Res plants (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data in Figure 7D showing reduced viral RNA accumulation.

claim: AGO1 over-expression could rescue the deficiency of ago18 for viral resistance.
source: Thus, AGO1 over-expression could rescue the deficiency of ago18 for viral resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AGO1a-Res expression in ago18 background restores viral resistance.

claim: AGO18 functions through sequestering miR168 to up-regulate AGO1 against virus infections.
source: These data provided further compelling evidence that AGO18 functions through sequestering miR168 to up-regulate AGO1 against virus infections.
evidence: Supported by the rescue of ago18 susceptibility by miR168-resistant AGO1a expression.

claim: AGO18 regulates AGO1 homeostasis by specifically loading miR168 during viral infection.
source: Based on the above results, we conclude that AGO18 regulates AGO1 homeostasis by specifically loading miR168 during viral infection.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including IP-Northern blots, deep sequencing, and complementation experiments.

claim: Sequestering of miR168 by AGO18 leads to increased accumulation of AGO1 to embark on an effective antiviral defense response.
source: Sequestering of miR168 by AGO18 leads to increased accumulation of AGO1 to embark on an effective antiviral defense response.
evidence: Supported by data showing AGO1 levels increase when AGO18 sequesters miR168, and this correlates with increased viral resistance.

claim: RSV CP is an effector to induce AGO18 expression during viral infection.
source: We found that AGO18 was induced only in the transgenic lines that over-expressed CP, but not in those that over-expressed three other viral proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This suggests that RSV CP is an effector to induce AGO18 expression during viral infection.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing AGO18 induction only in CP-overexpressing lines.

claim: AGO1a and 1b are expressed at much higher levels than AGO1c and 1d in both mock-inoculated and RSV-infected rice plants.
source: Since AGO1a and 1b are expressed at much higher levels than AGO1c and 1d in both mock-inoculated and RSV-infected rice plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) (Kapoor et al., 2008), we presumed that AGO1a and 1b are more important for antiviral defense.
evidence: Supported by microarray data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and citation to Kapoor et al., 2008.

claim: AGO1a and 1b are more important for antiviral defense than AGO1c and 1d.
source: Since AGO1a and 1b are expressed at much higher levels than AGO1c and 1d in both mock-inoculated and RSV-infected rice plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) (Kapoor et al., 2008), we presumed that AGO1a and 1b are more important for antiviral defense.
evidence: Inferred from the higher expression levels of AGO1a and 1b compared to AGO1c and 1d.

claim: The rice genome encodes five DCLs and 19 AGOs.
source: The rice genome encodes five DCLs and 19 AGOs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of rice genome annotation.

claim: Infection of many viruses can elevate the miR168 level to down-regulate AGO1, thereby nullifying this layer of host defense.
source: Moreover, infection of many viruses can elevate the miR168 level to down-regulate AGO1, thereby nullifying this layer of host defense (Várallyay et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Várallyay et al., 2010.

claim: Some plant viruses have evolved silencing suppressors to target AGO1.
source: As a counter-defense strategy, some plant viruses have evolved silencing suppressors to target AGO1 (Burgyán and Havelda, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burgyán and Havelda, 2011.

claim: AGO1 and AGO2 appear to exert antiviral functions in a non-redundant and cooperative manner.
source: AGO2 is repressed by AGO1-associated miR403, and AGO1 and AGO2 appear to exert antiviral functions in a non-redundant and cooperative manner. Specifically, AGO1 functions in the first layer of antiviral RNAi; when AGO1's antiviral function is inhibited, a second layer is activated involving AGO2 (Harvey et al., 2011; Jaubert et al., 2011; Scholthof et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Carbonell et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Harvey et al., 2011; Jaubert et al., 2011; Scholthof et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Carbonell et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2014.

claim: AGO1 functions in the first layer of antiviral RNAi; when AGO1's antiviral function is inhibited, a second layer is activated involving AGO2.
source: Specifically, AGO1 functions in the first layer of antiviral RNAi; when AGO1's antiviral function is inhibited, a second layer is activated involving AGO2 (Harvey et al., 2011; Jaubert et al., 2011; Scholthof et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Carbonell et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Harvey et al., 2011; Jaubert et al., 2011; Scholthof et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Carbonell et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2014.

claim: The model plant Arabidopsis thaliana encodes four DCLs that function in distinct and yet overlapping RNAi pathways to control diverse biological processes ranging from development, response to abiotic stresses, to defense against pathogens.
source: For instance, the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana encodes four DCLs that function indistinct and yet overlapping RNAi pathways to control diverse biological processes ranging from development, response to abiotic stresses, to defense against pathogens (Deleris et al., 2006; Chapman and Carrington, 2007; Garcia-Ruiz et al., 2010; Vazquez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deleris et al., 2006; Chapman and Carrington, 2007; Garcia-Ruiz et al., 2010; Vazquez et al., 2010.

claim: Arabidopsis encodes 10 AGOs whose functions are not all understood.
source: Arabidopsis encodes 10 AGOs whose functions are not all understood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Arabidopsis genome.

claim: AGO1 mediates mRNA cleavage and is critical for development.
source: Well-studied AGOs include AGO1 that mediates mRNA cleavage is critical for development, AGO4 that directs DNA methylation, and AGO2 that functions in DNA double strand break repair (Baumberger and Baulcombe, 2005; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010; Ye et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baumberger and Baulcombe, 2005; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010.

claim: AGO4 directs DNA methylation.
source: Well-studied AGOs include AGO1 that mediates mRNA cleavage is critical for development, AGO4 that directs DNA methylation, and AGO2 that functions in DNA double strand break repair (Baumberger and Baulcombe, 2005; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010; Ye et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ye et al., 2012.

claim: AGO2 functions in DNA double strand break repair.
source: Well-studied AGOs include AGO1 that mediates mRNA cleavage is critical for development, AGO4 that directs DNA methylation, and AGO2 that functions in DNA double strand break repair (Baumberger and Baulcombe, 2005; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010; Ye et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al., 2012.

claim: The AGO1 mRNA is a target of miR168.
source: At the post-transcriptional level, the AGO1 mRNA is a target of miR168.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of AGO1 regulation.

claim: miR168-guided cleavage of AGO1 mRNA by AGO1 protein exerts auto-regulation.
source: Therefore, miR168-guided cleavage of AGO1 mRNA by AGO1 protein exerts auto-regulation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of AGO1 auto-regulation mechanism.

claim: AGO1 is co-expressed with miR168 and AGO1 protein can stabilize miR168 post-transcriptionally.
source: Moreover, AGO1 is co-expressed with miR168 and AGO1 protein can stabilize miR168 post-transcriptionally (Vaucheret et al., 2006; Vaucheret, 2008; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vaucheret et al., 2006; Vaucheret, 2008; Mallory and Vaucheret, 2010.

claim: The accumulation of AGO1 can be reduced by F-box proteins in a proteasome-independent manner through the autophagy pathway.
source: At the post-translational level, the accumulation of AGO1 can be reduced by F-box proteins in a proteasome-independent manner through the autophagy pathway (Derrien et al., 2012; Rogers and Chen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Derrien et al., 2012; Rogers and Chen, 2013.

claim: RNA-mediated immunity against viruses operates in plants, fungi, invertebrates, and mammals to specifically destroy viral RNAs through the cellular RNA silencing machinery.
source: RNA-mediated immunity against viruses operates in plants, fungi, invertebrates, and mammals to specifically destroy viral RNAs through the cellular RNA silencing machinery (Li et al., 2013b; Maillard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2013b; Maillard et al., 2013.

claim: Rice viral pathogens are genetically diverse and many highly pathogenic viruses such as Rice stripe Tenuivirus (RSV, with a genome comprising 4 negative-stranded RNAs) and Rice dwarf Phytoreovirus (RDV, with a genome comprising 12 double-stranded RNAs) are transmitted persistently and solely by arthropod vectors.

claim: Engineering rice and other cereals to over-express AGO18 may provide a new strategy for the control of diverse viral pathogens.
source: We propose that engineering rice and other cereals to over-express AGO18 may provide a new strategy for the control of diverse viral pathogens.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings showing AGO18 overexpression confers broad-spectrum virus resistance.

claim: The up-regulation of AGO1 via AGO18 binding of miR168 represents a novel type of mechanism among mechanisms of AGO-regulation of AGO1 homeostasis or activity.
source: Thus, among mechanisms of AGO-regulation of AGO1 homeostasis or activity, the up-regulation of AGO1 via AGO18 binding of miR168 represents a novel type of mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previously known mechanisms of AGO regulation.

claim: In addition to miR168, several miRNAs including miR528, miR159a, and miR159b were also recruited by AGO18 in RSV-infected rice plants.
source: It is also noteworthy that, in addition to miR168, several miRNAs including miR528, miR159a, and miR159b were also recruited by AGO18 in RSV-infected rice plants (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data in Supplementary file 1C.

claim: AGO18 may play regulatory roles in other capacities or have its own independent biological functions.
source: Thus, for AGO18, we cannot rule out the possibility that AGO18 plays regulatory roles in other capacities or has its own independent biological functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that AGO18 binds multiple miRNAs beyond miR168.

claim: Sequestering miR168 by AGO18 to regulate AGO1 homeostasis represents an evolutionary novelty.
source: Finally, sequestering miR168 by AGO18 to regulate AGO1 homeostasis represents an evolutionary novelty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of evolutionary biology.
